title: Palliative and end of life care for children (NICE NG61)
blurb: Use an Advance Care Plan, manage pain by weight and recognise the last days of life in children, in line with NICE NG61, while supporting the whole family.
question: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting neurodegenerative condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes it means 'do not resuscitate'. What should the nurse be told?

teach.body: Children's palliative care can last years, often alongside active treatment, and involves the whole family. Formally, NICE NG61 covers end of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions, from diagnosis to death and bereavement. Plain English: plan ahead together, keep the child comfortable, honour where the family want care to happen, and support parents, brothers and sisters before and after the death.

rows.label: Who has one?
values: Every child with a life-limiting condition

values: Wishes, care, communication, place of care

teach.caption: NG61 1.2.14: an Advance Care Plan should not be confused with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order. 1.3.1: attempt resuscitation unless a DNACPR order is in place.

letters.word: Advance Care Plan, shared at each update
Network: MDT across hospital, hospice, home

teach.caption: After an antenatal diagnosis, Advance Care Planning can begin in pregnancy.

steps.label: Moderate to severe
steps.sub: Low-dose oral, transmucosal, SC or IV (central line) opioid

teach.caption: Non-drug measures too: reduce noise, music, touch, holding, massage, warm or cold packs, sucrose for neonates (1.3.25).

head: Rule
Recommendation
teach.caption: Many of these uses are off-label in children; explain this to families.

teach.h: Signs of the last hours or days (1.3.57)

cells.label: Less interest in food or drink

teach.caption: Also a marked, unexplained fall in urine output. Monitor non-invasively and interpret against the child's usual baseline.

teach.h: Fluids, place of death and home care
teach.body: Encourage a dying child to drink if they want to and can, and keep giving mouth care. If they cannot drink, discuss whether tube or IV fluids are in their best interests, as these can be a burden and may change where care happens (1.3.48–1.3.52). Agree the preferred place of care and death, which can change; consider rapid transfer if death is near (1.3.15). At home, services should offer day-and-night specialist advice and children's nursing (1.5.9).

teach.text: Do not dose a child's opioid from a standard 'age' table at the end of life. Children approaching death are often underweight for their age, so NG61 1.3.32 says calculate by weight. And anticipatory doses before a dressing change are not added in when working out the daily background dose.

teach.h: Scenario: Ella, 13, on a children's ward
teach.body: Ella may die within a day or two. Her Advance Care Plan records that she wants to die at home with her dog. Nurse Hana recognises noisy, irregular breathing and cool, grey hands. She tells the named consultant, who agrees rapid transfer is possible and in Ella's interest. Hana updates the Advance Care Plan with the community team, arranges anticipatory medicines and 24-hour nursing at home, and gives the family written information about what to expect and about bereavement support.

items: Every child with a life-limiting condition: Advance Care Plan and a named medical specialist.
An Advance Care Plan is not a DNACPR order; without a DNACPR, attempt resuscitation.
Stepwise analgesia; opioids titrated, dosed by weight, with breakthrough and anticipatory doses.
Know the signs of the last days: breathing change, poor perfusion, less intake, altered awareness.
Day-and-night support at home; written information on practical arrangements and bereavement.

summary: You can now explain and use an Advance Care Plan, manage pain stepwise with weight-based opioids, and recognise when a child may be in the last days of life. You can also plan place of death, hydration and home support, and care for the family before and after death.

A.q: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes it means 'do not resuscitate'. What is correct?
options: An Advance Care Plan is a DNACPR order
It means resuscitate in hospital settings
It means resuscitation needs parental consent
An Advance Care Plan is not a DNACPR order
A.why: NG61 1.2.14: every child with a life-limiting condition should have an Advance Care Plan, which should not be confused with a DNACPR order. Resuscitation is attempted unless a DNACPR order is in place (1.3.1).

whyNot.0: The two documents are different; NG61 warns against confusing them.
whyNot.1: The plan does not set location-based resuscitation rules.
whyNot.2: Without a DNACPR order, resuscitation is attempted.

A.q: Ahmed, 9, has a life-limiting condition and sees neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology and community teams. His parents feel nobody is in charge. What does NG61 recommend?
options: The GP leads all care
A named medical specialist coordinates
Each specialist leads their own area
The parents coordinate between teams
A.why: NG61 1.2.2: every child with a life-limiting condition should have a named medical specialist who leads and coordinates their care.

whyNot.0: The GP is involved, but NG61 specifies a named medical specialist.
whyNot.2: Separate leads are what leaves parents feeling nobody is in charge.
whyNot.3: Coordination is a professional role, not the parents' burden.

A.q: Sophie is 22 weeks pregnant. A scan shows her baby has a life-limiting condition and she plans to continue the pregnancy. When can Advance Care Planning begin?
options: After the baby is born
When the baby is first admitted
During the pregnancy
At the first sign of deterioration
A.why: Advance Care Planning can begin in pregnancy after an antenatal diagnosis of a life-limiting condition.

whyNot.0: Waiting until birth misses the chance to plan care at and after delivery.
whyNot.1: Planning should not wait for a hospital admission.
whyNot.3: Planning ahead is the purpose; waiting for deterioration defeats it.

B.q: Ruby, 11, is approaching the end of life with cancer and weighs 22 kg, much less than average for her age. How should her opioid dose be calculated?
options: By her age, using the BNFC age band
By the adult dose reduced by half
By her height and age combined
By her weight in kilograms
B.why: NG61 1.3.32: calculate opioid doses for children approaching the end of life using weight rather than age, because they may be underweight.

whyNot.0: Age-based dosing would overestimate her dose.
whyNot.1: Halving an adult dose is not a recognised method.
whyNot.2: Height is not the recommended basis.

B.q: Leo, 8, has background oral morphine. He also has 2 anticipatory doses before daily dressing changes. The team is reviewing his daily background dose. How should the anticipatory doses be treated?
options: Left out of the background total
Added to the background total
Doubled and added in
Replaced by a higher background dose
B.why: NG61 1.3.31: do not include anticipatory doses when calculating the required daily background dose.

whyNot.1: Including them would overestimate the background requirement.
whyNot.2: Doubling has no basis in the guidance.
whyNot.3: Predictable pain is better covered by anticipatory doses than a higher constant dose.

B.q: Grace, 7, is dying at a children's hospice. She takes small sips of water but can no longer drink much. Her parents ask about a drip. What does NG61 recommend?
options: Start IV fluids for every dying child
Discuss whether fluids are in her best interests
Stop all drinks to avoid aspiration
Insert a nasogastric tube at once
B.why: NG61 1.3.48–1.3.52: support drinking if wanted, continue mouth care, and discuss whether tube or IV fluids are in the child's best interests, as they can be a burden and may change the place of care.

whyNot.0: Fluids are an individual best-interests decision, not routine.
whyNot.2: She should be supported to drink if she wants and is able.
whyNot.3: Tube feeding is discussed, not started automatically.

C.q: Noah, 4, is on a children's ward in the last days of life. His breathing has become irregular and noisy, his hands are grey and cool, and he is less responsive. His parents ask what is happening. What should the nurse explain?
options: These are signs he may be in the last hours or days
These suggest a new infection needing antibiotics
These are side effects of his morphine
These are signs he is improving
C.why: NG61 1.3.57: changed breathing pattern, impaired peripheral perfusion and altered awareness are common in the last hours or days of life.

whyNot.1: In context, these match the dying process rather than a new treatable infection.
whyNot.2: Opioids do not explain the combination of perfusion and breathing changes described.
whyNot.3: These are not signs of improvement.

C.q: Ella, 13, may die within a day or two. Her Advance Care Plan records that she wants to die at home. She is on a children's ward. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep her on the ward as death is close
Wait for a bed at the local hospice
Ask her parents to decide without Ella
Raise rapid transfer home with the team and family
C.why: NG61 1.3.15: if a child may die soon and is not in their preferred place, think about whether rapid transfer is possible and in their best interests, and discuss it with them and their family.

whyNot.0: Closeness to death is a reason to consider rapid transfer, not to rule it out.
whyNot.1: The hospice is not her recorded preferred place of death.
whyNot.2: Ella should be involved in decisions about her care.

C.q: Jamal, 10, is being cared for at home at the end of life. His mother asks what help she can get at 3 am if his pain suddenly worsens. What should services provide under NG61?
options: Specialist advice in office hours
An ambulance call for any problem
Advice and nursing day and night
A GP appointment the next morning
C.why: NG61 1.5.9: children cared for at home at the end of life should have access to specialist advice and paediatric nursing care at any time, day and night.

whyNot.0: Office-hours support leaves gaps at night.
whyNot.1: Emergency services are not the planned route for symptom control.
whyNot.3: A next-day appointment does not meet the need for urgent night-time support.

reteach.title: Plan, comfort, accompany
reteach.question: What does good end of life care look like for a child and family?

blocks.body: Plan: an Advance Care Plan (not a DNACPR order) and a named medical specialist, with the preferred place of care and death agreed. Comfort: stepwise pain relief, opioids by weight, non-drug comfort, mouth care, fluids decided on best interests. Accompany: 24-hour support at home, written information about what happens after death, and bereavement support for parents and siblings.

root.label: Death may be close
root.sub: Where does the child want to be?

blocks.text: Having an Advance Care Plan does not mean resuscitation is withheld. Unless there is a DNACPR order, resuscitation is attempted.

explain.body: Recorded for every child with a life-limiting condition at an appropriate time. It includes contacts, who gives consent, the condition, how to communicate with the child, and wishes for care. It is shared with everyone each time it is updated (1.2.5, 1.2.12).

test.q: An Advance Care Plan for a child is updated. What does NG61 say should happen next?
options: Share it with everyone involved
File it in the hospital record
Send it to the GP on discharge
Keep it with the parents
test.why: NG61 1.2.12: share the Advance Care Plan with everyone involved each time it is updated.

whyNot.1: Filing it does not share it with community, hospice or school teams.
whyNot.2: The GP needs it, but so does everyone involved, at each update.
whyNot.3: Parents hold a copy, but all professionals involved should have it too.

explain.body: Mild pain: paracetamol or ibuprofen, then both. Moderate to severe: low-dose oral, transmucosal, SC or IV opioid. Titrate to the minimal effective dose, with background and breakthrough doses. Neuropathic pain: specialist-guided gabapentin, amitriptyline, ketamine or methadone.

test.q: Kai, 9, has neuropathic pain at the end of life despite standard analgesia. Which option does NG61 suggest, under specialist guidance?
options: Codeine
Aspirin
Gabapentin
Diclofenac
test.why: NG61 1.3.33: for neuropathic pain not helped by standard analgesia, consider gabapentin, low-dose amitriptyline or an anti-NMDA agent such as ketamine or methadone, with specialist guidance.

whyNot.0: Codeine is not a neuropathic agent and has restrictions in children.
whyNot.1: Aspirin is not given to under-16s unless prescribed for specific indications.
whyNot.3: Diclofenac is not listed for neuropathic pain in NG61.

explain.body: Common signs: noisy, laboured or irregular breathing; pale or grey skin and long CRT; temperature instability; loss of interest in food and drink; a marked fall in urine output; altered awareness. Monitor non-invasively, judged against the child's baseline.

test.q: Which change is listed in NG61 as common in the last hours or days of life?
options: A sudden rise in urine output
Increased appetite
A marked fall in urine output
Warm, pink peripheries
test.why: NG61 1.3.57 lists a marked and unexplained fall in urine output among the common signs.

whyNot.0: Urine output falls rather than rises.
whyNot.1: Interest in food and drink is usually lost.
whyNot.3: Peripheral perfusion is usually impaired, with pale or grey skin.

explain.body: Give parents written information on practical arrangements: care of the body, the coroner where relevant, the child death review process, registration, funeral and post-mortem. Discuss bereavement support. Every child death is reviewed by child death review partners (local authority and ICB).

test.q: A child dies at home after a long illness. Which information does NG61 say parents should receive in writing?
options: Practical arrangements after the death
The family's hospital bill
A list of other bereaved families
The full medical record
test.why: NG61 1.4.1: discuss practical arrangements after the death (care of the body, legal matters including child death review, coroner, registration, funeral, post-mortem) and provide them in writing.

whyNot.1: NHS care is not billed to families.
whyNot.2: Contact details of other families would breach confidentiality.
whyNot.3: Records can be requested, but this is not the NG61 recommendation.
